claim: Lipoic acid is a highly conserved organosulfur cofactor found in all three domains of life.
source: Lipoic acid (1,2-dithiolane-3-pentanoic acid or 6,8-thioactic acid, Figure 1) is a highly conserved organosulfur cofactor found in all three domains of life.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the distribution of lipoic acid across life forms.

claim: Only five lipoate-dependent multienzyme complexes have been characterized: three α-ketoacid dehydrogenases (pyruvate dehydrogenase, 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase), acetoin dehydrogenase and the glycine cleavage complex.
source: So far, only five lipoate-dependent multienzyme complexes have been characterized: three α-ketoacid dehydrogenases (pyruvate dehydrogenase, 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase), acetoin dehydrogenase and the glycine cleavage complex (Cronan, 2016; Cronan et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature reviews.

claim: In lipoylated enzyme complexes, lipoate acts both as an electrophile that binds to reaction intermediates and as a swinging arm that channels the bound substrate between the active sites of different subunits.
source: In the five characterized lipoylated enzyme complexes, lipoate acts both as an electrophile that binds to reaction intermediates (via a thioester or thioether bond) and as a swinging arm that channels the bound substrate between the active sites of different subunits.
evidence: This describes the established mechanistic role of lipoate in known enzyme complexes.

claim: During catalysis, the intramolecular disulfide bond of lipoate cycles between oxidized lipoamide and reduced dihydrolipoamide.
source: During catalysis, the intramolecular disulfide bond of lipoate cycles between oxidized lipoamide and reduced dihydrolipoamide (Figure 1) (Reed and Hackert, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1 showing the chemical structures.

claim: A large group of archaeal and bacterial sulfur oxidizers utilize a novel pathway of sulfur oxidation involving a heterodisulfide reductase (Hdr)-like enzyme complex.
source: Comparative genome mining of sulfur-oxidizing prokaryotes (Dahl, 2015; Quatrini et al., 2009; Venceslau et al., 2014), transcriptomic and proteomic studies (Latorre et al., 2016; Mangold et al., 2011; Osorio et al., 2013; Ouyang et al., 2013; Quatrini et al., 2009) as well as first biochemical evidence (Boughanemi et al., 2016) indicated that a large group of archaeal and bacterial sulfur oxidizers utilize a novel pathway of sulfur oxidation involving a heterodisulfide reductase (Hdr)-like enzyme complex resembling the HdrABC (Wagner et al., 2017) of methanogens, although a coenzyme M-coenzyme B (CoM-S-S-CoB) heterodisulfide is not present in the sulfur oxidizers.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and biochemical studies.

claim: The Hdr-like complex is essential for oxidation of thiosulfate to sulfate in Hyphomicrobium denitrificans.
source: Recently, we provided conclusive genetic evidence that this complex is indeed essential for oxidation of thiosulfate to sulfate in Hyphomicrobium denitrificans (Koch and Dahl, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior genetic evidence.

claim: A Δhdr strain of H. denitrificans was unable to grow on dimethylsulfide (DMS).
source: In this Alphaproteobacterium, thiosulfate is an intermediate of dimethylsulfide (DMS) degradation and a Δhdr strain was also unable to grow on the volatile organosulfur compound (Koch and Dahl, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Sulfur-oxidizing prokaryote genes encoding the Hdr-like complex are associated with genes encoding novel lipoate-binding proteins resembling GcvH.
source: The sulfur-oxidizing prokaryote genes (hdrC1B1A-hyp-hdrC2B2) encoding the Hdr-like complex are associated with genes encoding novel lipoate-binding proteins resembling GvcH, the lipoate-binding component of the bacterial glycine cleavage system (Ehrenfeld et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies identifying these gene associations.

claim: Database searches revealed 56 different cultivated genome-sequenced prokaryotes from one archaeal and six bacterial phyla as containing typical hdr-like gene loci.
source: Database searches revealed 56 different cultivated genome-sequenced prokaryotes from one archaeal and six bacterial phyla as containing typical hdr-like gene loci (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: With very few exceptions all organisms containing hdr-like gene loci are either established chemo- and photolithotrophs oxidizing reduced inorganic sulfur compounds or they have been reported as oxidizing mineral sulfides or volatile organic sulfur compounds.
source: With very few exceptions all these organisms are either established chemo- and photolithotrophs oxidizing reduced inorganic sulfur compounds or they have been reported as oxidizing mineral sulfides (FeS, FeS2 and others) or volatile organic sulfur compounds (e.g. dimethylsulfide).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the organisms identified in the database search.

claim: In all cases, the cluster of hdr-like genes is associated with at least one, in most cases with two and in a few cases with three genes for putative lipoate-binding proteins resembling classical glycine cleavage system H (GcvH) proteins.
source: In all cases, the cluster of hdr-like genes is associated with at least one, in most cases with two and in a few cases with three genes for putative lipoate-binding proteins resembling classical glycine cleavage system H (GcvH) proteins (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: In almost all cases, the hdr-lbpA arrangement is linked in the same gene cluster structure with genes encoding proteins probably involved in the biosynthesis of lipoate binding proteins.
source: In almost all cases, the hdr-lbpA arrangement is linked in the same gene cluster structure with genes encoding proteins probably involved in the biosynthesis of lipoate binding proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on genomic analysis of gene cluster organization.

claim: The close genomic association of lipoate-binding proteins with maturation enzymes indicates the possibility of a specific biosynthetic pathway required for maturation of Hdr-associated lipoate-binding proteins.
source: The close genomic association of lipoate-binding proteins with maturation enzymes together with the observation that virtually all organisms analyzed contain enzymes catalyzing the canonical pathways for biosynthesis of lipoylated proteins (Figure 2—source data 1) indicate the possibility of a specific biosynthetic pathway required for maturation of Hdr-associated lipoate-binding proteins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genomic organization patterns observed.

claim: All LbpA proteins share a strictly conserved lysine residue known to be required for lipoate attachment.
source: All these proteins share a strictly conserved lysine residue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) known to be required for lipoate attachment (Spalding and Prigge, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation to prior knowledge.

claim: With the exception of some archaeal LbpAs, the most conspicuous common features of the new LbpA proteins are two strictly conserved cysteine residues that GcvH proteins lack.
source: With the exception of some archaeal LbpAs, the most conspicuous common features of the new LbpA proteins are two strictly conserved cysteine residues that GcvH proteins lack, one cysteine is located near the N-terminus whereas the other is close to the C-terminus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of LbpA proteins encoded in group I gene clusters clearly showed two distinct types of LbpA proteins, LbpA1 and LbpA2.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of LbpA proteins encoded in group I gene clusters (Figure 3) clearly showed two distinct types of LbpA proteins, LbpA1 and LbpA2.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: In all organisms containing two lbpA genes, one gene encodes an LbpA1 and the other a member of the LbpA2 type.
source: In all organisms containing two lbpA genes, one gene encodes an LbpA1 and the other a member of the LbpA2 type (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: TsLbpA1 and HdLbpA2 eluted as monomers of the expected sizes by analytical gel permeation chromatography.
source: TsLbpA1 and HdLbpA2 were analyzed by analytical gel permeation chromatography and eluted as monomers of the expected sizes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Thiorhodospira TsLbpA1 analyzed by mass spectrometry yielded a value 17,457 Da which matched that of the unmodified apoprotein.
source: Thiorhodospira TsLbpA1 was analyzed by mass spectrometry and yielded a value 17,457 Da which matched that of the unmodified apoprotein.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Pure LbpA2 protein produced under anoxic conditions at low temperature migrated significantly faster than the unmodified apoprotein obtained by IPTG-induced expression from a pET-based plasmid.
source: Indeed, pure LbpA2 protein produced under these conditions migrated significantly faster than the unmodified apoprotein obtained by isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG)-induced expression from a pET-based plasmid (Figure 4, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In H. denitrificans cell extracts, the fast migrating band was clearly identified as being lipoylated because it was detected by an antibody directed specifically against HdLbpA2 as well as by an anti-lipoic acid antibody.
source: In H. denitrificans cell extracts, the fast migrating band was clearly identified as being lipoylated because it was detected by an antibody directed specifically against HdLbpA2 as well as by an anti-lipoic acid antibody (Figure 4, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Comparative proteomics indicated specific formation of proteins encoded in the hdr-lbpA2 gene cluster during growth on DMS.
source: Comparative proteomics indicated specific formation of proteins encoded in the hdr-lbpA2 gene cluster during growth on DMS (Koch and Dahl, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior proteomic work.

claim: Western blotting verified the presence of a lipoylated protein of the expected size in cells grown on methylamine/thiosulfate but its absence in cells grown on the organic compound alone.
source: Western blotting using two different antibodies, one directed against H. denitrificans LbpA2 and the other against lipoic acid, verified this finding and furthermore proved the presence of a lipoylated protein of the expected size in cells grown on methylamine/thiosulfate but its absence in cells grown on the organic compound alone (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The H. denitrificans ΔlbpA strain was incapable to grow on or degrade dimethylsulfide.
source: Phenotypic analyses unambiguously revealed that the ΔlpbA strain was incapable to grow on or degrade dimethylsulfide (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth and substrate consumption data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The lbpA2-deficient H. denitrificans strain showed a clear phenotype when thiosulfate was provided as an additional electron source during chemoorganoheterotrophic growth on methanol.
source: In addition, the lbpA2-deficient H. denitrificans strain showed a clear phenotype when thiosulfate was provided as an additional electron source during chemoorganoheterotrophic growth on methanol (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: While the wild type produced sulfate from thiosulfate, H. denitrificans ΔlbpA2 formed tetrathionate.
source: While the wild type produced sulfate from thiosulfate (Figure 5B, middle panel), H. denitrificans ΔlbpA2 formed tetrathionate, just as observed for hdrA insertional mutant (Koch and Dahl, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by sulfur compound analysis data shown in Figure 5B and a citation.

claim: The GcvH-like LbpA2 protein is an indispensable component of the Hdr-like pathway of sulfur oxidation.
source: In summary, our findings demonstrate that the GcvH-like LbpA2 protein is an indispensable component of the Hdr-like pathway of sulfur oxidation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic deletion experiments showing loss of sulfur oxidation function.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, the glycine cleavage system protein GcvH plays a central role in the modification biosynthesis of other lipoic acid requiring enzymes.
source: In Bacillus subtilis, the glycine cleavage system protein GcvH plays a central role in the modification biosynthesis of other lipoic acid requiring enzymes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about B. subtilis lipoate metabolism.

claim: In B. subtilis strain NM20, disruption of gcvH resulted in complete loss of biosynthetic lipoyl assembly pathway and the ∆gcvH strain became a lipoate auxotroph.
source: In B. subtilis strain NM20, disruption of gcvH resulted in complete loss of biosynthetic lipoyl assembly pathway and the ∆gcvH strain became a lipoate auxotroph (Christensen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neither LbpA1 nor LbpA2 could restore growth of the B. subtilis ∆gcvH strain.
source: No discrete colony formation was observed even with induction of IPTG indicating that neither LbpA1 nor LbpA2 could restore growth of the B. subtilis ∆gcvH strain (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No octanoylated LbpA1 or LbpA2 band was observed in LipM modification assays.
source: No octanoylated LbpA1 or LbpA2 band was observed suggesting the failure of in vivo complementation was due to lack of modification by LipM.
evidence: This claim is supported by autoradiography data from in vitro assays.

claim: Neither of the novel lipoate-binding proteins is able to functionally replace the B. subtilis GcvH protein as a hub in octanoyl group transfer.
source: Hence we conclude that neither of the novel lipoate-binding proteins is able to functionally replace the B. subtilis GcvH protein as a hub in octanoyl group transfer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complementation and in vitro modification experiments.

claim: The E. coli ΔlipB ΔlplA strain QC146 is unable to grow with lipoic acid supplementation.
source: Due to the E. coli QC146 ΔlplA mutation, the strain is unable to grow with lipoic acid supplementation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the E. coli mutant strain phenotype.

claim: Upon expression of the putative lplA-encoding genes from sulfur compound oxidizers, the E. coli strain failed to grow, either in the presence or in the absence of lipoic acid.
source: Upon expression of the putative lplA-encoding genes from sulfur compound oxidizers, the E. coli strain failed to grow, either in the presence or in the absence of lipoic acid.
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation assay data.

claim: The proteins cannot serve as lipoate ligases for E. coli lipoate cognate proteins in the presence of free lipoate and they fail to act as octanoyl transferases in the E. coli background.
source: This indicates that the proteins cannot serve as lipoate ligases (at least not for E. coli lipoate cognate proteins) in the presence of free lipoate and that they fail to act as octanoyl transferases in the E. coli background (data not shown).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complementation experiments.

claim: E. coli LD was readily lipoylated in the presence of lipoic acid and ATP by S. coelicolor LplA.
source: We found that, E. coli LD was readily lipoylated in the presence of lipoic acid and ATP by S. coelicolor LplA as shown by the faster migration on native gel electrophoresis due to loss of the positive lysine charge upon modification (Hermes and Cronan, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel shift assay data and a citation.

claim: LplA from H. denitrificans and Thioalkalivibrio sp. K90mix had no activity with E. coli LD.
source: However, LplA from H. denitrificans and Thioalkalivibrio sp. K90mix had no activity with E. coli LD (Figure 6E, top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: LplA-like proteins encoded in hdr-like gene cluster have activity only upon their natural cognate proteins, which are the LbpA proteins encoded by the closely linked genes.
source: Given our findings that the novel LbpA proteins from sulfur oxidizers could not be modified by other lipoate metabolism proteins and that in turn LplA-like proteins from sulfur oxidizing bacteria fail to show lipoylation activity with the E. coli cognate proteins, we hypothesized that LplA-like proteins encoded in hdr-like gene cluster have activity only upon their natural cognate proteins, which are the LbpA proteins encoded by the closely linked genes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the specificity observed in prior experiments.

claim: Synthesis of both octanoyl-adenylate and lipoyl-adenylate intermediates were readily demonstrated by use of ATP labeled in the α-phosphate.
source: In the absence of an acceptor protein, synthesis of both octanoyl-adenylate and lipoyl-adenylate intermediates were readily demonstrated by use of ATP labeled in the α-phosphate (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by TLC analysis data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Upon addition of an acceptor protein, LbpA1 or LbpA2, the adenylate intermediates were hydrolyzed to AMP.
source: Moreover, upon addition of an acceptor protein, LbpA1 or LbpA2, the adenylate intermediates were hydrolyzed to AMP. This was readily observed by the increased formation of AMP.
evidence: This claim is supported by TLC analysis data.

claim: Lipoylated Lbp proteins had a mass increase of about 185 Da for both Lbp proteins (184.5 Da for LbpA1 and 186.2 for LpbA2) comparing with the unmodified forms.
source: Lipoylated Lbp proteins had a mass increase of about 185 Da for both Lbp proteins (184.5 Da for LbpA1 and 186.2 for LpbA2) comparing with the unmodified forms (17457.1 Da for LbpA1 and 16410.7 for LbpA2) (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by MALDI mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: The mass increases matched well with the expected value (188 Da) upon addition of a lipoyl group.
source: The mass increases matched well with the expected value (188 Da) upon addition of a lipoyl group.
evidence: This is an inference comparing observed mass changes to expected values.

claim: LbpA and LplA-like proteins encoded in or close to hdr-like gene clusters exhibit cross-species functionality.
source: Gel mobility shift assays showed that LbpA and LplA-like proteins encoded in or close to hdr-like gene clusters exhibit cross-species functionality (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The LplA-like protein from Thioalkalivibrio sp. K90mix lacked the small domain and only had a single large domain, which aligns very well with the large catalytic domain of E. coli LplA.
source: Upon threading the lipoate ligase of Thioalkalivibrio sp. K90mix onto the known E. coli LplA structure (PDB: 3A7R), we found to our surprise that the LplA-like protein lacked the small domain and only had a single large domain, which aligns very well with the large catalytic domain of E. coli LplA (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: These enzymes provide an exception to the canonical rule that a conventional lipoate-protein ligase should have two domains in order to catalyze the two partial reactions.
source: Hence, these enzymes provide an exception to the canonical rule that a conventional lipoate-protein ligase should have two domains in order to catalyze the two partial reactions (activation of lipoic acid to lipoyl-AMP and transferring the lipoate moiety from lipoyl-AMP to its cognate proteins).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis showing single-domain architecture.

claim: The LplA-like protein from the sulfur oxidizer lacked octanoyl transferase activity regardless of whether LbpA1 or LbpA2 were present as acceptor proteins.
source: After autoradiographic analysis, we found that the LplA-like protein from the sulfur oxidizer lacked octanoyl transferase activity regardless of whether LbpA1 or LbpA2 were present as acceptor proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by autoradiography data from octanoyl transferase assays.

claim: The Thioalkalivibrio LplA-like protein has only lipoate (or octanote) scavenge activity and plays no role in de novo lipoyl assembly.
source: Therefore, the Thioalkalivibrio LplA-like protein has only lipoate (or octanote) scavenge activity and plays no role in de novo lipoyl assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the octanoyl transferase assay results.

claim: The universal occurrence of lbpA in all hdr-like gene clusters in conjunction with the genetic evidence establish the lipoate-binding proteins as key components in the novel Hdr-like pathway of sulfur oxidation.
source: The universal occurrence of lbpA in all hdr-like gene clusters (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1) in conjunction with the genetic evidence presented, establish the lipoate-binding proteins discovered in this study as key components in the novel Hdr-like pathway of sulfur oxidation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genomic analysis and genetic deletion experiments.

claim: A biological function was established for the universally conserved cofactor lipoate that is markedly different from its canonical roles in central metabolism.
source: Here, deletion of the gene identified LbpA as an essential component of the Hdr-like sulfur-oxidizing system in the Alphaproteobacterium Hyphomicrobium denitrificans. Thus, a biological function was established for the universally conserved cofactor lipoate that is markedly different from its canonical roles in central metabolism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and biochemical evidence showing lipoate's role in sulfur oxidation.

claim: LbpAs likely function as sulfur-binding entities presenting substrate to different catalytic sites of the Hdr-like complex, similar to the substrate-channeling function of lipoate in carbon-metabolizing multienzyme complexes.
source: LbpAs likely function as sulfur-binding entities presenting substrate to different catalytic sites of the Hdr-like complex, similar to the substrate-channeling function of lipoate in carbon-metabolizing multienzyme complexes, for example pyruvate dehydrogenase.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanistic role of LbpAs based on analogy to known lipoate functions.

claim: LbpAs serve a specific function in sulfur oxidation, cannot functionally replace the related GcvH protein in Bacillus subtilis and are not modified by the canonical E. coli and B. subtilis lipoyl attachment machineries.
source: LbpAs serve a specific function in sulfur oxidation, cannot functionally replace the related GcvH protein in Bacillus subtilis and are not modified by the canonical E. coli and B. subtilis lipoyl attachment machineries.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from complementation and modification assays.

claim: LplA-like lipoate-protein ligases encoded in or in immediate vicinity of hdr-lpbA gene clusters act specifically on LbpA proteins.
source: Instead, LplA-like lipoate-protein ligases encoded in or in immediate vicinity of hdr-lpbA gene clusters act specifically on these proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro lipoylation assays showing specificity.

claim: In most prokaryotes specialized for lithotrophic growth on reduced inorganic sulfur compounds, the initial steps occur outside of the cytoplasm.
source: In most prokaryotes specialized for lithotrophic growth on reduced inorganic sulfur compounds like sulfide or thiosulfate, the initial steps occur outside of the cytoplasm (Dahl, 2015; Venceslau et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior reviews.

claim: The LpbA protein is a prime candidate as a sulfur substrate-binding entity that might present the sulfur substrate to different catalytic sites of the Hdr-like complex.
source: The LpbA protein is a prime candidate as a sulfur substrate-binding entity that might present the sulfur substrate to different catalytic sites of the Hdr-like complex.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanistic role of LbpA.

claim: In vitro studies with bovine and one microbial rhodanese showed that dihydrolipoate can serve as sulfane sulfur acceptor.
source: This idea is corroborated by in vitro studies with bovine and one microbial rhodanese showing that dihydrolipoate can serve as sulfane sulfur acceptor (Cianci et al., 2000; Silver and Kelly, 1976; Villarejo and Westley, 1963a, 1963b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: The presence of lipoate as a key cofactor in the Hdr-like sulfur-oxidizing system bears the possibility that two of the four electrons released in the catalyzed reaction are used to generate dihydrolipoamide during the reaction cycle.
source: As depicted in Figure 8, the presence of lipoate as a key cofactor in the Hdr-like sulfur-oxidizing system bears the possibility that two of the four electrons released in the catalyzed reaction (R-S-S- + 3 H2O → R-S- + HSO3- + 5 H+) are used to generate dihydrolipoamide during the reaction cycle.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the electron flow in the reaction mechanism.

claim: The electrons released upon reoxidation of dihydrolipoamide can be directly transferred onto NAD+.
source: Since the lipoamide/dihydrolipoamide system possesses one of the lowest standard biological redox potentials (E0'=−0.29 V), the electrons released upon reoxidation of dihydrolipoamide can be directly transferred onto NAD+.
evidence: This is an inference based on known redox potentials.

claim: This reaction could considerably reduce the need for energy-demanding reverse electron flow in lithoautotrophic sulfur oxidizers.
source: This reaction could considerably reduce the need for energy-demanding reverse electron flow in lithoautotrophic sulfur oxidizers.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the bioenergetic implications.

claim: A gene for a bona fide dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase is tightly linked with the hdr-gene cluster in sulfur oxidizing archaea.
source: In fact, a gene for a bona fide dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase is tightly linked with the hdr-gene cluster in sulfur oxidizing archaea (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior genomic analysis.

claim: The lipoate-binding proteins studied in this work are specifically designed for sulfur oxidation.
source: The lipoate-binding proteins studied in this work are specifically designed for sulfur oxidation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the specificity observed in complementation and modification experiments.

claim: The LbpA proteins from sulfur oxidizers do not serve as substrates for the biosynthetic machineries involved in lipoate-binding protein maturation in B. subtilis and E. coli.
source: The LbpA proteins from sulfur oxidizers do not serve as substrates for the biosynthetic machineries involved in lipoate-binding protein maturation in B. subtilis and E. coli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modification assays.

claim: The first biosynthetic protein characterized in vitro from the sulfur oxidizers, an LplA-like lipoate-protein ligase does not recognize lipoyl domains/proteins from organisms lacking components of a Hdr-like sulfur-oxidizing system.
source: On the other hand, the first biosynthetic protein characterized in vitro from the sulfur oxidizers, an LplA-like lipoate-protein ligase does not recognize lipoyl domains/proteins from organisms lacking components of a Hdr-like sulfur-oxidizing system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro lipoylation assays.

claim: Such specificity is unprecedented, usually protein substrates are interchangeable in vitro.
source: Such specificity is unprecedented, usually protein substrates are interchangeable in vitro (Cao and Cronan, 2015; Cao et al., 2018; Christensen and Cronan, 2010; Posner et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies showing substrate promiscuity.

claim: All sulfur oxidizers analyzed in this study contain the genetic equipment for lipoate-protein biosynthesis via previously established pathways.
source: All sulfur oxidizers analyzed in this study contain the genetic equipment for lipoate-protein biosynthesis via previously established pathways (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: These biosynthetic routes appear to be employed exclusively for the known lipoate-binding components of 2-oxoacid dehydrogenases and glycine cleavage systems.
source: These biosynthetic routes appear to be employed exclusively for the known lipoate-binding components of 2-oxoacid dehydrogenases and glycine cleavage systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity observed in modification experiments.

claim: The LpbA proteins involved in sulfur oxidation differ so much from GvcH proteins that they are not recognized by the GvcH maturation enzymes but are specifically modified by lipoate-protein ligases encoded in the same gene cluster.
source: The LpbA proteins involved in sulfur oxidation obviously differ so much from GvcH proteins that they are not recognized by the GvcH maturation enzymes but are specifically modified by lipoate-protein ligases encoded in the same gene cluster.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modification and complementation experiments.

claim: TkLplA is an active lipoyl/octanoyl ligase despite lacking the small C-terminal domain seen in all other lipoate ligases studied to date.
source: Our finding that TkLplA is an active lipoyl/octanoyl ligase despite lacking the small C-terminal domain seen in all other lipoate ligases studied to date was unexpected.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis and activity assays.

claim: Both domains are required for the overall reaction and for lipoyl-adenylate formation whereas only the large domain was required for transfer of lipoate from the adenylate to the acceptor protein.
source: Prior work showed that both domains are required for the overall reaction and for lipoyl-adenylate formation whereas only the large domain was required for transfer of lipoate from the adenylate to the acceptor protein (Cao and Cronan, 2015; Christensen and Cronan, 2010; McManus et al., 2006; Posner et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The most straightforward hypothesis is that the lipoate-binding proteins LbpA1 and LbpA2 not only act as lipoate acceptors but also have a motif that triggers the conformational change usually engendered by the small domain.
source: The most straightforward hypothesis is that the lipoate-binding proteins LbpA1 and LbpA2 not only act as lipoate acceptors but also have a motif that triggers the conformational change usually engendered by the small domain.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain the activity of single-domain ligases.

claim: This could explain the inability of either the HdLplA/TkLplA ligase or LbpA1 and LbpA2 binding proteins to interact with the ligases and acceptor domains of central metabolism proteins of other bacteria.
source: If so, this could explain the inability of either the HdLplA/TkLplA ligase or LbpA1 and LbpA2 binding proteins to interact with the ligases and acceptor domains of central metabolism proteins of other bacteria.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed specificity.
